tagline: The cheap CRM that is really a doorway into fifty other Zoho apps.
verdictSummary: For one person, Zoho CRM Standard is leads, contacts, deals, custom fields, workflow rules and reports — and every one of those is ordinary software you can build, which is why this is a kinda rather than a no. The moat is not in the CRM, it is in the suite around it: the moment you also want Zoho Books, Desk and Campaigns talking to each other, twenty dollars buys wiring nobody rebuilds. The build here takes a week because the reporting layer, done properly, is most of the work.
coreLoopDIY: Run the pipeline, then get real answers out of it: reports defined as readable SQL views, scheduled into an email digest so the numbers arrive without anyone opening the CRM.
whatYouLose: the rest of the Zoho suite and the one-click connections between its apps
the marketplace of several hundred CRM extensions
email and telephony integration inside the record
workflow rules and blueprints configured by clicking rather than by writing code
whyPeopleStillPay: Because Zoho's pitch is that every other business tool you will need is already next door at the same price, and moving from CRM to invoicing to helpdesk costs a click instead of an integration project.
prompt:
Build a CRM whose reporting layer is the main event, not an afterthought.

Stack: Postgres specifically — the design depends on it — plus your choice of server framework and Docker Compose.

CRM core, kept plain: Lead, Contact, Account, Deal, Activity. Leads convert into a Contact plus an Account plus optionally a Deal, in one transaction, keeping a link back to the originating lead. Deals have stage, amount, close date, owner. Every stage change writes an immutable history row.

The reporting layer:
- Reports are defined as named SQL views in a migrations folder, one file per report, each with a comment at the top explaining in one sentence what question it answers. Ship five: pipeline by stage, deals won and lost by month, average sales cycle, activities per owner per week, and leads by source with conversion rate.
- The app lists available reports by reading the view catalogue, runs them with an optional date-range parameter, and renders the result as a table with CSV download. No query builder UI — if you want a new report you write a view, and the README explains how.
- Any report can be scheduled: pick a report, a cron expression and recipients, and the app emails the rendered table on that schedule. Use a local mail transport in development and document the production setup.

Security boundary worth getting right: reports run as a database role with SELECT only, on a connection separate from the application's. Say so in the README.

Also include: custom fields per entity, saved list views with filters, tags, CSV import with mapping, and full-text search.

Write tests for lead conversion (idempotent, no orphaned records) and for the scheduler firing exactly once per due window after a restart.

Do not build marketing automation, telephony, or a helpdesk. This is the CRM, and the README should say plainly that the rest of the Zoho suite has no equivalent here.

faq.q: Why are reports SQL views instead of a report builder?
faq.a: Because a report builder is weeks of work that produces worse queries than you would write by hand, and because a view with a comment at the top is readable, diffable and reviewable. It also means a wrong number can be traced to a specific file.

faq.q: Is this really a fair substitute for Zoho CRM?
faq.a: For a solo user on the Standard tier, close — the feature list at that tier is pipeline, custom fields, reports and workflow rules. For anyone using Zoho as a suite, no: the value of Zoho is the neighbours, and this build has no neighbours.

Left out, and that is the biggest honest gap after the suite. Zoho lets a non-developer say "when a deal reaches Negotiation, create a task and email the owner" by clicking. Here that is a piece of code you write, or a webhook you wire to something else.

faq.q: How painful is getting data out of Zoho CRM?
faq.a: Not very. Every module exports to CSV, and there is a full data backup that produces a zip of everything. The awkward parts are attachments and the audit trail, which come out in shapes that are hard to import anywhere else.
